title: More: How Much AI Art Is Being Used
text:
Across our two datasets, AI art usage grew from a small niche in early 2021 into hundreds of thousands of shared works by early 2023:

Social media AI art (TWIGMA): 797,203 AI-generated art posts tracked in monthly totals from January 2021 through March 2023 (from an overall release of 805,650 images), generating 15,188,062 total likes. Monthly volume jumped from 789 posts in January 2021 to 211,851 posts in March 2023.
Benchmark AI art (AI-ArtBench): 125,000 AI-generated images (12,500 per style across 10 major art movements) produced with Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion.

title: Other: How Much Physical Art Has Been Used
text:
In the ArtBench-10 / AI-ArtBench dataset, 60,000 human-made physical artworks are used as the foundational benchmark for traditional art. To ensure every artistic movement is equally represented without bias toward a single era, the dataset curates exactly 6,000 physical artworks in each of 10 historical styles from public museum and gallery archives (WikiArt, Ukiyo-e.org, and Surrealism.website).
By contrast, AI-ArtBench pairs those 6,000 physical artworks per style against 12,500 AI-generated artworks per style—more than double the physical count in every category.

title: About
text:
Data Sources and Collection
This project combines two public research datasets found in November 2026 to compare the rise of AI-generated artwork with human-made physical artwork.

1. TWIGMA (Zenodo)

Where and when it was found: Hosted on Zenodo (Record 8031785), originally published in 2023 (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track) by Stanford researchers Yiqun T. Chen and James Zou, and accessed for this project in November 2026.
How they got the data: The researchers collected roughly 2.2 million tweets posted on Twitter/X between January 2021 and March 2023 that matched generative-AI art hashtags and keywords (such as #dalle, #stablediffusion, #midjourney, and #aiart). After filtering out duplicates and non-AI images, they compiled 805,650 AI-generated artworks along with post dates and engagement metrics (such as likes).



2. AI-ArtBench & ArtBench-10 (Kaggle)

Where and when it was found: Hosted on Kaggle (AI-ArtBench and ArtBench-10), built on Peiyuan Liao et al.’s 2022 ArtBench-10 benchmark and expanded into AI-ArtBench in 2023, accessed for this project in November 2026.
How they got the data:

Physical (human-made) artworks (60,000 images): Curated by Liao et al. (UC Berkeley and CMU) from public online art archives—primarily WikiArt.org, Ukiyo-e.org (Japanese woodblock prints), and Surrealism.website—cleaned and balanced to include exactly 6,000 artworks across each of 10 historical art styles.
AI-generated artworks (125,000 images): Created by prompting Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion models to generate synthetic artworks matching those same 10 historical art styles.

title: Fun Facts
text:
AI Art Grew Nearly 269x in Just Two Years: Monthly AI art posts in TWIGMA jumped from just 789 in January 2021 to 211,851 in March 2023—meaning a single month of AI art sharing produced more than 3.5 times the entire 60,000-artwork physical benchmark.
Surrealism Was AI Art’s Favorite Classical Style: Among the 10 historical art movements tracked in TWIGMA, Surrealism appeared most often (606 posts)—more than eight times as often as runner-up Renaissance (72 posts), fitting how early AI generators excelled at dreamlike, uncanny imagery.
Centuries of Physical Art, Balanced to the Exact Artwork: The 60,000 human-made artworks in ArtBench-10 span centuries and continents—from Japanese Ukiyo-e woodblock prints to Baroque and Impressionism paintings—curated to 6,000 pieces per style so no single era outweighs another.
800,000+ AI Artworks Sifted from 2.2 Million Tweets: To create TWIGMA (short for Twitter Generative-AI Images), Stanford researchers filtered roughly 2.2 million tweets down to 805,650 verified, non-duplicate AI artworks that earned 15,188,062 total likes across our monthly series.
AI-ArtBench Outnumbers Physical Art 2-to-1 on Purpose: Researchers paired 12,500 AI-generated images (from Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion) against 6,000 physical artworks in every style (125,000 AI vs. 60,000 physical) specifically to train computer-vision models to tell human brushwork apart from AI pixels.
